query: For multi-component concentrated alloys, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs their strength and deformation or failure behavior, and why? Specify a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing cause, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the conditions over which the hypothesis should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The mechanical response (strength and deformation behavior) of multi‐component concentrated alloys is governed primarily by the spatial fluctuations in their generalized planar fault energies—arising from local chemical short‐range order (SRO) and lattice distortion—rather than by their averaged values. These local fluctuations create a rugged energy landscape that forces dislocations into wavy, segmented paths with higher activation barriers (via nanoscale segment detrapping), leading to enhanced yield strength and work hardening.
generation.material_initial_state: An FCC-based multi-component concentrated alloy (e.g., equiatomic CrCoNi) in an as-annealed state that exhibits pronounced local chemical ordering and inherent lattice distortions.
generation.intervention: Process identical alloy compositions with two different treatments: (1) a thermal treatment designed to promote and retain SRO (thus maximizing local fault-energy fluctuations) and (2) severe plastic deformation or high-temperature homogenization to randomize the local order and reduce fluctuations.
generation.conditions: Ambient temperature tensile tests under controlled strain rates on FCC-based high- or medium-entropy alloys (e.g., CrCoNi or related compositions) where atomic size differences and cohesive energy variations are substantial; the hypothesis is expected to hold when the alloy remains in a single-phase solid solution.
generation.structural_mediator: Local variations in generalized stacking/shear fault energies, mediated by the degree of chemical short-range order and lattice distortion.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced local fluctuations increase the energy barrier required for dislocation movement by creating a rugged energy landscape. Dislocations are forced to follow wavy paths and must overcome variable local pinning points (nanoscale segment detrapping), which increases the yield strength and work-hardening rate. When the local order is randomized, these fluctuations diminish, lowering the energy barriers for dislocation motion.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys processed to retain strong local chemical order (and hence, prominent fault-energy fluctuations) will exhibit a higher yield strength and increased work-hardening compared to otherwise identical alloys processed to randomize the local order, even though both have similar average fault energies.
generation.baseline: The performance of the alloy processed with heavy deformation (or high-temperature randomization) to reduce SRO, serving as a baseline with minimal local fault-energy fluctuations.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to be valid for FCC-based multi-component concentrated alloys with significant atomic mismatch and inherent lattice distortion. Its applicability may be limited in alloys where the overall atomic size differences are low, in non-FCC structures, or where additional deformation mechanisms (such as prevalent twinning or phase transformations) dominate the response.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative magnitude of the strengthening effect attributable solely to local fault-energy fluctuations remains uncertain, and there may be overlapping contributions from other mechanisms (e.g., deformation twinning, phase transformation) that need to be separately identified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples from the same alloy composition. One set should be thermally treated to promote and retain local chemical short-range order (SRO), while the other set should undergo severe plastic deformation or high-temperature treatment to randomize the SRO. Perform detailed tensile tests and microscopy (e.g., TEM or atom probe) to assess the degree of local fault-energy fluctuations.
measurements: Stress-strain curves to determine yield strength and work-hardening rates
Quantitative microstructural analysis (e.g., TEM, APT) to assess SRO and local fluctuation in fault energies
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloy samples with pronounced local SRO (and thus high fault-energy fluctuations) do not show a statistically significant increase in yield strength and work-hardening compared to the randomized samples—despite clear differences in local ordering—then the hypothesis that local fluctuations govern the enhanced strength would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: SignificanceComplex concentrated alloys (CCAs) with multi elements in equiatomic ratios are exotic alloys but what governs their strength is currently not clearly understood. This work has proven the prime origin of strength in CCAs as arising from the fluctuations (not the averaged value) of the shear-fault energy, which is an important feature of CCAs unrecognized beforehand. Through identification of the local hard atomic motifs far beyond the traditional concept of the globally averaged short-range ordering parameters, this work has unfolded the physical basis of strength in CCAs and provides important clues for designing high-strength CCAs by focusing on the alloy composition to produce large fault-energy fluctuations. Local chemical short-range ordering (SRO) and spatial fluctuations of planar fault energy are important features of multi-element and metastable complex concentrated alloys (CCAs). Arising from them, dislocations in such alloys are distinctively wavy in both static and migrating conditions; yet, such effects on strength have remained unknown. We report multi-component high-entropy materials as extraordinarily robust diffusion barriers and clarify the highly suppressed interdiffusion kinetics in the multi-component materials from structural and thermodynamic perspectives. The failures of six alloy barriers with different numbers of elements, from unitary Ti to senary TiTaCrZrAlRu, against the interdiffusion of Cu and Si were characterized, and experimental results indicated that, with more elements incorporated, the failure temperature of the barriers increased from 550 to 900°C. The activation energy of Cu diffusion through the alloy barriers was determined to increase from 110 to 163 kJ/mole. Mechanistic analyses suggest that, structurally, severe lattice distortion strains and a high packing density caused by different atom sizes, and, thermodynamically, a strengthened cohesion provide a total increase of 55 kJ/mole in the activation energy of substitutional Cu diffusion, and are believed to be the dominant factors of suppressed interdiffusion kinetics through the multi-component barrier materials.

High-entropy and medium-entropy alloys are presumed to have a configurational entropy as high as that of an ideally mixed solid solution (SS) of multiple elements in near-equal proportions. However, enthalpic interactions inevitably render such chemically disordered SSs rare and metastable, except at very high temperatures. Here we highlight the wide variety of local chemical ordering (LCO) that sets these concentrated SSs apart from traditional solvent-solute ones. Using atomistic simulations, we reveal that the LCO of the multi-principal-element NiCoCr SS changes with alloy processing conditions, producing a wide range of generalized planar fault energies. We show that the LCO heightens the ruggedness of the energy landscape and raises activation barriers governing dislocation activities. This influences the selection of dislocation pathways in slip, faulting, and twinning, and increases the lattice friction to dislocation motion via a nanoscale segment detrapping mechanism. In contrast, severe plastic deformation reduces the LCO towards random SS. Multi-principal-element alloys have been assumed to have the configurational entropy of an ideal solution. cited_evidence.kind: web:Strategy to design HEAs with large strength and ductility via SRO
cited_evidence.text: We performed iterative MC and MD simulations to examine the evolution of SRO in the CoCuFeNiPd HEA and MD simulations to investigate the effect of SRO on mechanical behavior. During the formation of SRO, some small regions transform to BCC-preferred structures (BCC is more stable than FCC), while others become very strongly FCC-preferred structures (FCC is much more stable than BCC). The resulting structure is a pseudo-composite microstructure consisting of very stable FCC-preferred (FCCP) regions and BCC-preferred (BCCP) regions in a matrix of marginal stability. Tensile-deformation simulations indicate that the ultimate strength and ductility of the HEA are both enhanced by the development of the SRO. The origin of these enhancements can be traced to the SRO-induced pseudo-composite microstructure that forms; this consists of both FCCP hardening domains and BCCP toughening domains in a matrix of marginal phase stability. We propose a strategy for simultaneously achieving excellent strength and ductility via SRO in HEAs.
